kessef_hakodashim.he: סעיף ד' (המוכר לחבירו דרך) יד בעל השטר על התחתונה אם כתוב שיור דריסת הרגל אין בכך משא בבהמה גם באחת. ואולי די באמה רוחב שכ"ה רוחב גוף. ואם כתוב כל מקום החצר לדריסת הרגל שייך בכל רחבו ומכל מקום י"ל שלא במשא בבהמה. ואם כתוב גם במשא י"ל דקאי בבהמה כי בלא בהמה לא הי' צריך לפרט משא. ומכל מקום י"ל רק בבהמה אחת. ובפרט במקנה דריסת הרגל שמשייר בעין יפה היטב. ואולי יש לומר דכיון דהמשאוי בהרחבה יותר מהנושא י"ל דהיינו בטיעון כנהוג ומכל מקום שלא בבהמה ואם כתוב בבהמה י"ל ולא בעגלה: כתוב דריסת הרגל ופרה לחליבה כיון דנהוג לילך בשעת חליבה י"ל דצ"ל רוחב לדרהר"ג ופרה בשעת חליבה. ודרהר"ג בעגלה טעונה יש לו יותר משיעור רוחב עגלה כי צ"ל מהלך בצידה ומשאה לפעמים מרחיב הרבה מהעגליה וצ"ל כפי שייכות רוחב הנהוג לפעמים: שטר שכתוב בו זכות דריסת הרגל בכל מה שקורין פיר הויז ולא כתוב בו משער לשער לעבור בהם אולי יכול המקנה לומר בכל מה שבין השערים הקניתי לך ולא ברשותי שחוצה לשניהם רק שער א' איזה שארצה בו יש לך לכנוס ולצאת שכולל ממילא דרהר"ג לך בגבולי שחוץ להבנין ולא בשער השני כי יד בעל השטר על התחתונה. וגם אם פתח א' קרוב אליו יכול ליתן לו רשות רק בהרחוק לבד: שטר שכתוב בו שמה שקורין פיר הויז שבין ב' בתים. אשר אחד מהבתים מכור ללוקח וכתוב ללוקח שיהי' שניהם שווים בשימוש בהפיר הויז. ואחר כך כתוב ובידו גם כן להעמיד לו שם אלמיר בצד כותלו. וטוען הלוקח שרק הוא יעמיד ולא המוכר. אין זה טענה כי שימוש שוה כ"ה נכון ומ"ש רשות להעמיד כו'. הוצרך לכך כי לולא מפורש והי' הי' צד לומר שלשימוש קבוע בהעמדה הממעט שם שימוש בשום פעם אין רשות. וממילא כיון דהלוקח יכול להעמיד לא גרע ממנו המוכר ומשייר בעין יפה משייר. גם הלשון ג"כ להעמיד תיבת כן מורה שההעמדה היא כן כשמוש שהם שווים גם מספק יש חזקת מרא קמא:
kessef_hakodashim.en: Seif 4. One who sells his fellow a right of passage. The holder of a document has the weaker hand. If a deed reserves only a right of foot passage, it does not include transporting a load by animal, perhaps not even by one animal, and possibly a width of one cubit suffices because that is approximately a person's bodily width. If the deed grants passage throughout the courtyard, the right may extend across its width, but still not necessarily with a loaded animal. If it explicitly mentions a load, that likely refers to transport by animal, because otherwise there was no need to specify a load, though perhaps only one animal is included. This is especially so where the grantor reserved the right for himself, since a person who reserves rights generally does so generously. Since a load may project wider than the bearer, the wording may perhaps include the ordinary width required for carrying a load, though still not necessarily an animal. If the deed says passage with an animal, it may still not include a wagon. If it grants foot passage and a cow for milking, since one ordinarily walks beside the cow while milking arrangements are made, enough width must be allowed for a person and the cow at that time. A right of passage for a loaded wagon requires more than the wagon's width, because a person must be able to walk beside it and the load may project beyond it; the width should follow ordinary practical usage. If a deed grants a right of passage in an entry hall between gates but does not say 'from gate to gate,' the grantor may perhaps say that he granted passage only within the hall, and outside it the grantee may use whichever one gate the grantor chooses for entry and exit, because the holder of the deed has the weaker hand. Even if one opening is nearer the grantee, the grantor might permit only the farther one. If a deed states that an entry hall between two houses, one sold to the purchaser, is to be used equally by both parties, and then adds that the purchaser may also place a cupboard beside his wall, the purchaser cannot argue that only he may place one and the seller may not. Equal use remains the governing rule. The additional clause was necessary because without it one might have thought that no one could place a permanent object that reduces the other's use. Once the purchaser is expressly allowed to do so, the seller who retained his rights is certainly no worse, especially because a person who reserves rights does so generously. The word 'also' likewise indicates that the right to place the cupboard follows the same equal-use arrangement. In any event, doubt leaves the original owner in possession.

להשקות בה בקילון. כ"כ גם כן בטור בקילון ובמיימוני כתוב " בסילון "בסמ"ך וכן ציינו המ"מ וכתב עליו ז"ל אבן מאג"ש פי' שהוא מקום מעבר מי רגלים ומי תכבוסת של חצירו וכן פי' ר"ש שהוא עשוי להשקות ממנו בהמה ורוחצין ממנו בגדים וכלים ואינם גדולים כ"כ עכ"ל המ"מ ומשמעות ל' המ"מ הוא דשני הפירושים הוא על נוסחות "סילון ולולי פי' המ"מ היה נראה לומר דר"ש לנוסחאות קילון דוקא כתב פירושו ע"ש בפ' המוכר פירות (בבא בתרא דף צ"ט ע"ב) דשם במימרא דשמואל כתוב קילון וז"ל ר"ש אמת הסילון איכא דאמרי קילון ולהשקות בהמות כו' דמדכתב ולהשקות בוי"ו משמע דלמ"ד קילון דסמך ליה קאי:
meirat_einayim.en:
The place of the water channel. The buyer needs to dig an irrigation channel through the seller's field in order to water his irrigated field, which requires much water. The seller must therefore give him a strip of land through the field four cubits wide along the entire length in which the channel is to run: two cubits for the channel itself and one cubit on each side for its banks. So writes the Rambam. The Tur, however, says that he gives one cubit for the width of the channel and two cubits for the banks. Rashbam likewise records a version that reads this way and writes that this is the primary text. According to that version it is called an amah because the channel itself is one cubit wide. I wrote in the Perishah that the Rosh's textual version also appears to support this. It is surprising that Rama did not mention this opinion at all.
To irrigate with it by a small channel. The Tur likewise reads “by a kilon,” while Maimonides reads “by a silon” with a samekh. The Maggid Mishneh notes this and writes in the name of Ibn Migash that it means a channel through which the wastewater and laundry water of the courtyard passes. Rashbam similarly explains that it is used to water animals and to wash clothes and utensils, and is therefore not as large as an ordinary irrigation channel. The Maggid Mishneh's wording implies that both explanations apply to the reading “silon.” Were it not for his explanation, it would appear that Rashbam's explanation belongs specifically to the reading “kilon.” See Bava Batra 99b, where Shmuel's statement reads “kilon,” and Rashbam writes, “the channel of the silon, some say kilon, and for watering animals,” etc. The conjunction suggests that his explanation follows the reading immediately preceding it.

For he accepted it on that understanding, etc. The Gemara asks why the field owner cannot say, “The water in your channel caused the banks to collapse.” It answers that ordinarily one who sells a place within his field for digging a water channel agrees from the outset that if the banks collapse, earth may be taken from his field to repair them. Otherwise, where would the purchaser obtain repair earth? Must he transport soil from another place? This is the Mechaber's ruling.

The Maggid Mishneh writes that the Mechaber's words require study, for he mentions only one burial cave. According to the end of the Mishnah, even according to the Sages one makes a courtyard six by six cubits and opens two caves into it, as the Rashbam explains. It appears that Rambam understands the latter clause as a case where one expressly undertook to make a courtyard, but this requires study. The Beit Yosef writes that Rambam held the latter clause applies only according to Rabbi Shimon. I do not understand this either, for Rabbi Shimon disputes the latter clause as well.

meirat_einayim.en: Thus between each grave and the graves at its sides there is one and a half cubits. The diagram follows the Rambam's interpretation. Rashbam and the Tur understand the layout differently. In the Perishah I gave their explanation and diagram as well. The Rambam and Mechaber abbreviate the baraita, which says that one makes a cave four by six, etc., and a courtyard at its entrance six by six, and makes another cave like it on the opposite side of the courtyard. The Maggid Mishneh and Beit Yosef question why the Rambam omitted parts of this arrangement. In the Derishah I offered some resolution.

baer_hetev.en: The grave. Because the grave in which the deceased is buried is forbidden for benefit, the purchaser must therefore return its value to him. This is unlike the route to the grave and the place where the funeral assembly and eulogy are held. If the purchaser consents and says, 'Eulogize him there, and afterward I will take it back for my own use,' he cannot be displaced from it permanently. For this reason the text says only that they bury him there against the purchaser's will. Ibid.

He was slicked by his husband. They believe that the family will not be buryed in place as their custom:
And they give him the value of the grave. Since a grave in which a dead person is buried becomes prohibited for benefit, they must reimburse its value. This differs from a path or the place where people stand for the eulogy. If the purchaser agrees and says, “Use it for the eulogy and afterward I will reclaim it for my own use,” they cannot remove him from ownership of it. For this reason the rule says only that they bury the dead there against his will, not that the other areas are permanently taken from him.
